newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-A Marine called Tabatha breaks barriers.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-A Marine called Tabatha breaks barriers.

text.p: After a long hike over rugged terrain, toting her rifle and a backpack that weighs almost as much as she does, Tabatha Allen was thankful for a rest from her combat training alongside male Marines.

As the U.S. military grapples with gender issues ranging from sexual harassment and abuse to questions about women's ability to meet tough physical standards, the diminutive 25-year-old Reno, Nevada, native was among 106 women making clear their point of view:

"For years the women have been saying I can do that, I can do that, but proving it is really hard," Allen said. "Well, we're here. We're doing the same training as them and we're proving to everybody that we're not just saying we can do it, but we're proving that we can do it."

Allen spoke to Reuters recently as she took part in Operation Leatherneck at Camp Devildog near Camp Lejeune Marine Corps Base in Jacksonville, North Carolina. The women were the first to participate in the Marines Corps' newly integrated combat training programme, where women train alongside men.

The 17-day course began on March 18 and the pace was tough for Allen, who at 4 feet 9 inches (1.45 metres) and 90 pounds (41 kg) was the smallest Marine in the group. She took two or three steps to her longer-legged companions' one and the toll on her was clear. Blisters on her feet were covered with bandages.

But Allen said she knew she had what it takes to complete the training. Coming from a family of Marines -- taller ones at that -- she had already grown tough enough to withstand her relatives' telling her she was too small to make it.

Allen may never see actual combat. Women still are not allowed to participate in hand-to-hand fighting. But after the 1991 Gulf War, in which women were closer to the front line than ever before, the military rethought its training programmes.

Operation Leatherneck is part of Marine Commandant Gen. Charles Krulak's revamping in which non-infantry Marines, including women, get combat training. Female recruits at Parris Island, South Carolina, have been given a condensed version of this training but the two sexes are not trained together.

"In today's warfare it's awfully hard to determine what the front line would be," Col. James O'Donnell, commanding officer of the School of Infantry, said. "During Desert Shield (the Gulf War) some of the major casualties we had were in Dhahran, which was supposedly in the rear, but it got hit with a Scud and some National Guardsmen took a major hit there."

"I got to Saudi Arabia and saw women in virtually every area over there and the light went on," Lt. Col. Carl Cobb, Marine Combat Training Battalion commander, said. "I believe it is the right thing to do. If you're going to put females into potentially the same situation as males in terms of a hostile environment they ought to get the same training."

The training schedule is rigorous for both sexes, with 14 days in the field loaded down with heavy packs and driven to exhaustion. The recruits arrived a Camp Lejeune after a grueling 12 weeks of basic training at Parris Island. Men and women carry the same heavy packs and rifles.

"I think they (women) do just as well as the male Marines do," tactics instructor Sgt. William Blais said. "They're Marines. And we need to learn to train as Marines ... not as female Marine or male Marine, but as Marines, integrated."

Men and women are separated for some training such as digging foxholes but shoot together on the firing range. They crawl through an open field together learning to probe for mines, are taught to read maps and navigate unfamiliar land, to use night vision equipment and provide security at an airfield.
It is a tough two weeks, Wilmington, North Carolina, native Christina Bostic said. Like her father, who spent much of his duty at Camp Lejeune, Bostic plans to make the Marines a career.

"This proves I'm hard core," Bostic, 19, said. "To myself, not anyone else. I guess it's to be put on the same level as the men instead of under them. This changes it for all of us, to not be an outcast because we're females."
Putting on her helmet for another five-mile hike, Wisconsin native Erin Pitts was still filled with confidence from surviving 12 weeks of boot camp at Parris Island.

"It's exciting because we're accomplishing something that no one has ever accomplished before," she said. "It's very, very, very tough. Your feet hurt. Your back hurts. Anytime you want to quit, you dig deeper, find a little bit more to put out. It's overwhelming how much strength you really have that you would never guess that you have."
